title: The Bargain
note: Judgment entered on the Feast of Broken Vows.
subject: Lucian Voss
officials: Aurel, Keeper of the Highest Seat
Oriel, Warden of the Unending Decree
intro: Heaven did not condemn Lucian for treating people as entries in a ledger. Its ledger used much the same method. The court asked whose name he had placed at the head of every column.
counts: Unbelief concealed by patronage
Buying bishops and funding a cathedral did not excuse his private suspicion that no God was listening. The court demanded conviction as well as payment.
Prayer without an approved recipient
At nine, he had appealed to any listening power. Heaven entered the frightened child's uncertainty as an insult to its exclusive right to answer.
Withholding divine credit
He claimed to have built his fortune himself. Exploitation was treated as earthly administration; failing to thank God for the proceeds was sacrilege.
Mercy without conversion
Some hospital patients recovered without embracing the proper faith. Their survival counted for less than the missed opportunity to recruit worshippers.
Unauthorized ownership of praise
His name on charitable buildings competed with the Almighty's. Heaven objected to the signature, not to the suffering the gifts concealed.
verdict: Verdict: eternal torment, without credit for restitution. The court declined to hear the injured workers: their testimony could establish cruelty, but not wounded divine pride. Below, the ledger would finally count what Heaven had ignored.

title: The Pious
note: Judgment entered at the ninth bell of the Feast of the Scapegoat.
subject: Bishop Aurelius Vane
officials: Morael, Keeper of the Closed Gate
intro: Aurelius expected his obedience to purchase acquittal. Heaven praised the authority he had protected, then prosecuted the few occasions on which his conscience had exceeded his instructions.
counts: A question never fully extinguished
He had once wondered whether an infant could deserve damnation. Suppressing the question did not erase the fact that he had imagined God capable of injustice.
Rescue before reverence
During the flood, he had reached for a child before completing a prayer. Heaven called the interruption a declaration that a human life mattered more than its acknowledgment.
Goodness without sufficient attribution
The scholarship and the vigil beside a dying person included moments of unadvertised tenderness. The court found no explicit dedication of those moments to divine glory.
The wrong kind of love
He sometimes loved the congregation as people rather than as proof of God's dominion. Affection not routed through the throne was classified as theft.
Accepting rival devotion
Parishioners admired the bishop himself. Heaven counted their admiration against him while leaving his silencing of victims outside the indictment.
verdict: Verdict: eternal torment. His defense of abusive authority earned commendation, not a charge. Lena, Jonas and the others were unnecessary to this trial. Their names would become unavoidable only in the cathedral below.

title: The Accuser
note: Approximate date of the hearing; Satan's original exile predates recorded human history.
subject: Satan; the human cases on the returned docket
intro: The proceeding arrived with its conclusion already sealed. Satan's ancient condemnation was renewed, and the human witnesses were measured by the loyalty their testimony offered Heaven.
counts: Calling coerced worship loveless
Satan had asked whether praise extracted under threat could be love. The prosecution called the question rebellion because an answer would require the throne to justify itself.
Requesting evidence from authority
He demanded that accusation follow responsibility. Heaven treated scrutiny of its orders as a greater offense than obedience to an order to kill.
Refusing the appointed scapegoat
Returning cruelty to its human authors endangered the doctrine that Heaven remained innocent whenever its servants acted in its name.
Compassion without a command
The woman who sheltered an enemy child had not waited for permission. Her deed entered the docket as insubordination: she had trusted mercy before she trusted rank.
Belief in the wrong authority
The human cases were marked for unbelief, rival worship or insufficient submission. Massacre and starvation mattered chiefly when they embarrassed the throne.
verdict: Verdict: perpetual exile reaffirmed; eternal sentences entered on the human docket under the same test of allegiance. The hearing that follows challenges that record. Heaven calls obedience innocence; the returned accusations ask who actually chose the harm.

title: The Tribunal
note: Judgment entered on November 13, the Tribunal of Saints.
subject: Reverend Pell and the fallen congregation
officials: Adriel, Arbiter of the Single Way
Azriel, Bearer of the Final Seal
intro: Before the six judges below could hear a witness, Heaven issued one sentence for the entire congregation. It found their differences inconvenient. These are the heavenly officers, not the tribunal they later face in Hell.
counts: Worship conducted incorrectly
The final hymn used a disputed wording; some knelt at the wrong moment and others remained seated. The court treated errors of ceremony as refusals of sovereignty.
Compassion during sacred time
Ruth had fed Abram when devotion required her attendance elsewhere. Heaven called the bread a stolen offering and her absence a greater injury than his hunger.
Doubt beneath the roof
Several worshippers could no longer believe, though they still came to help their neighbors. Service without assent was ruled counterfeit goodness.
Loyalty to the wrong image
Members understood God differently. The court condemned mutually incompatible beliefs with equal certainty, offering no means by which a sincere mistake could be forgiven.
Taking pride in the sanctuary
Pell accepted praise for the church. Its dangerous repairs were secondary; the decisive offense was allowing admiration to stop at the minister instead of reaching God.
verdict: Verdict: eternal torment for all, with no distinction between secret generosity, frightened silence and deliberate harm. Heaven refused Ruth's mitigating evidence. The tribunal below must recover the individual choices that this collective sentence erased.

title: The Furnace Gospel
note: Decree entered during the Festival of Forbidden Knowledge; Caldus is still alive.
subject: Brother Caldus, Abbot Severin and the custodians
officials: Raziel, Custodian of the Authorized Word
Keziel, Binder of the Eternal Writ
intro: The warrant against Caldus was written in advance of his death. Heaven could not tolerate a living example of goodness surviving uncertainty. Its sentence awaited him while the furnace continued to burn.
counts: Writing “We do not know”
Caldus admitted the limits of a record. The court declared that an honest uncertainty weakened God's reputation more than a useful falsehood could.
Reading without permission
He examined discarded testimony. Truth obtained outside the approved chain of authority was charged as contamination, even when it exposed an injury.
Hearing the condemned
He listened to Nema before demanding a profession of faith. Heaven ruled that credibility belonged to allegiance, not to evidence.
Questioning divine authorship
He refused to call slaughter pacification. Correcting a text bearing sacred approval was prosecuted as correcting its supposed divine author.
Allowing silence after prayer
He would no longer manufacture certainty to fill an unanswered appeal. The court called this unbelief: God was entitled to an answer flattering to God.
Guarding a rival institution
Severin's censorship was praised, but his devotion to the abbey's prestige was condemned. Even obedient lies became sinful when their credit accrued to someone else.
verdict: Verdict: eternal torment, enforcement upon death; no appeal through later kindness. The story records Caldus's living resistance to that decree. Heaven wants an immaculate claim; the scriptorium below preserves the human cost of making it.

title: The Last Sermon
note: Unholy Night warning: December 24, c. 1987; final judgment about seven months later.
subject: Silas Creed
officials: Vadran, Steward of the Endless Sentence
intro: Heaven had tolerated forty years of profitable terror. The charges arrived after Silas began telling the truth. His Christmas warning was not his death; the final decree followed seven months of attempted repair.
counts: Apologizing to the injured first
He asked people for forgiveness before making their pain an occasion to praise God. Heaven named this a reversal of the proper order of importance.
Doubting the justice of damnation
He could no longer call endless punishment loving merely because authority commanded it. The court defined moral hesitation as a refusal to worship.
Abandoning useful fear
His confession weakened the machinery that had filled pews and raised money. A frightened believer counted more than an honest unbeliever.
Recognizing goodness outside the faith
He admitted that people he had condemned could be kinder than their accusers. Heaven called this an unauthorized route to human worth.
Loving without demanding assent
Reconciliation with Miriam was not made conditional on her submission. Love that did not recruit another worshipper was entered as disloyalty.
Giving up the sacred alibi
He ceased presenting prejudice and ambition as divine instructions. The resulting embarrassment to God's reputation outweighed every life his honesty might help.
verdict: Verdict: eternal torment, with no reduction for repentance directed toward real victims. Heaven punished the change that made him less cruel. Below, he would hear both the gratitude and the injury that an infallible throne had refused to distinguish.
